other_side: NLW's lead is that enterprise demand has grown up — buyers now argue about open-weights policy, routers and cost provisioning rather than counting their first two use cases — and that this new sophistication is what will finally kill AI washing. Zitron, publishing the same day, argues that the demand being celebrated is largely manufactured. Citing Barclays estimates, he puts OpenAI's and Anthropic's compute spend at around 73% of Amazon's AI revenues, and points to Wells Fargo's figure of roughly $3.9bn for Microsoft 365 Copilot across some 30 million paid seats — a per-seat number he reads as heavy discounting rather than pull. His conclusion is blunt: "the demand for AI-powered software is not there," and hyperscaler growth is mostly the big three funding their own largest customers in a circle.
truth_beneath: Both men orbit one variable: whether AI revenue from ordinary buyers — firms that are neither a frontier lab nor a lab's backer — is real and compounding. They agree on more than the tone suggests: that capex is enormous, that the labs' own compute spend is a large share of reported AI revenue, and that much announced enterprise AI is theatre. The empirical question is customer concentration, and the observable that settles it is a hyperscaler disclosing AI revenue net of OpenAI and Anthropic compute spend, alongside revenue per paid seat for embedded AI software. The residue is worldview: whether sophisticated procurement questions show real adoption or a better-dressed purchasing ritual. NLW is vindicated if non-lab AI software revenue grows materially; Zitron if that figure stays in the low tens of billions against a trillion in capex. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is that both now call the cost-cutting AI story a fiction. Watch whether any hyperscaler breaks out AI revenue by customer next quarter.
